card.hook: From across the valley, the Golden Bridge looks tiny, like a gold ribbon dropped on the mountainside. Then you spot the two giant stone hands holding it up, and you'll feel like you've found a secret.
card.stand_here: Stand in the grounds of Chùa Linh Ứng, the pagoda near the Golden Bridge area, and face south-east. The bridge lies that way, across the valley, with mountains and prayer flags around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the wide scene with the mountains and prayer flags. Then try 2x up to 5x (it depends on your phone) to bring the bridge closer. Use 0.5x only if you want a flag or the pagoda grounds big in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day and take the first cable car, around 7:00 to 8:00 AM, because fog often covers the view later. Check opening hours and any closures before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the terrace just outside the Golden Bridge cable car station, at the same level as the bridge, and use your front camera with the bridge behind you. For a moodier shot, stand close to one of the giant stone hands near the fingers and hold your phone a little below eye level.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on the observation deck behind the Starbucks store to take your photo, since it's roomy enough for groups and families.
card.rules_and_safety: Signs on the bridge warn you not to lean through the railings, so keep your phone and yourself on the right side. Drones are not permitted.
card.challenge: Get a prayer flag in the foreground with the bridge sitting on a gridline, and see if you can spot both stone hands.
card.good_to_know: The Golden Bridge (Cầu Vàng) is about 150 metres long and curves almost back on itself. The hands holding it up are built from fibreglass and wire mesh to look like stone. Construction ran from July 2017 to April 2018, and the bridge opened in June 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the grounds of Chùa Linh Ứng, the pagoda near the Golden Bridge area, and face south-east. The bridge lies that way, across the valley, with mountains and prayer flags around it.

selfie_research.safety: Signs along the bridge warn visitors not to lean through the railings, but a reviewer says some people ignore them.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found states any rule on selfie sticks or tripods, so the rules list is empty. One page (Vietnam Travels Online) says you can set a tripod at a spot on the bridge, but that is a tip, not a rule. Pages say drones are banned at Ba Na Hills, and FlyCam use needs a permit, but drones are outside this brief. The bridge is inside Sun World Ba Na Hills, not in central Da Nang; the given coordinates fit that location. Crowds are heavy from mid-morning, and mist can hide the view on some days. Some pages are older (one is about 2,488 days old), so the deck and terrace layout may have changed. The 'ask someone' deck is the one spot I could tie to a named landmark (the Starbucks store), so check it on a map before going.

card.hook: Five rocky hills shoot straight up out of flat land near the coast, like someone dropped them there. There's one spot where all five fit in a single photo, and it's worth the climb.
card.stand_here: Climb the steps up the west side of Thủy Sơn from Tam Thai Pagoda to Vọng Giang Đài, the stone pavilion. Stand in the pavilion and face back the way you came, over the five hills, with Non Nuoc Beach, the Co Co River and the Da Nang skyline behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so all five hills and the skyline squeeze in. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single hill or the beach.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the line of hills on the lower third, and let the sky and skyline fill the rest.
card.best_time: Sunrise or sunset gives you warm, soft light, and the pavilion photo is best taken first while the light is gentle. The site closes in the late afternoon, so sunset may fall after closing. Check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone archway at the entrance, with its carved stonework behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the carvings fill the frame over your shoulder. Early morning has softer light and smaller crowds.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps are narrow and steep, with little or no handrails, and they can be slippery, so take your time and keep one hand free. This is a religious and heritage site, so parts may be ticketed or restricted. Ask before photographing monks or altars.
card.challenge: Count the hills in your photo. Can you get all five in, plus a corner of the pavilion's stone edge in the foreground?
card.good_to_know: The Marble Mountains are also called Ngũ Hành Sơn, or 'five elements mountains'. Each hill is named after an element: metal, water, wood, fire and earth. Thủy Sơn is the one you can climb, up 156 steps to wide views, caves and shrines. The mountains were given National Special Relic status in January 2019, and the area is known for stone carving.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb the steps up the west side of Thủy Sơn from Tam Thai Pagoda to Vọng Giang Đài, the stone pavilion. Stand in the pavilion and face back the way you came, over the five hills, with Non Nuoc Beach, the Co Co River and the Da Nang skyline behind them.

selfie_spots.why: The first optimal location for photography in Marble Mountains is at the entrance. The beautiful stone archway with intricate carvings makes for a stunning backdrop. The best time to capture this spot is in the early morning when the light is soft and the crowds are smaller.

selfie_research.safety: Steps are narrow and steep with little-to-no handrails, and surfaces can be slippery, according to one visitor's account of climbing the mountain from inside.
selfie_research.notes: Sources conflict on tripods: one says tripods are not permitted in Am Phu Cave's narrow passages, another says tripods are allowed, and a third advises discretion; check on arrival. The Am Phu rule is only about that cave, not the whole site. One guide suggests bringing a selfie stick because of crowds, and shops sell them, but no page states a selfie-stick rule, so none is listed. No page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole landmark in frame, so that field is null. The second selfie spot is weaker: its source calls the courtyard a 'peaceful, green backdrop' but does not say which way the visitor should face. The Huyen Khong sunbeam is an interior light feature, not a backdrop for a selfie, so I left it out. The sources are blogs and tour pages of mixed dates, and I did not verify the spots on a map.

card.hook: Picture wet sand glowing gold, a round basket boat sitting on the shore, and nobody else in your shot. That's My Khe at sunrise, and it only lasts about an hour.
card.stand_here: Stand on the beach stretch in front of Võ Nguyên Giáp street, near the Fusion Maia resort entrance. Face the open sea, with Son Tra Peninsula in the distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the boats, wet sand and sea. Try 0.5x for the whole sweep of the shore, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one fisherman or one boat.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide the brightness down a little so the sunrise colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Be there about 5:45 AM from November to March, before the boats head out around 6:30 AM. Early morning is also calmer, because the beach gets busier in the late afternoon.
card.selfie_here: Walk up to the 'Da Nang Beach' sign on the promenade along the My Khe beachfront. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low, with the sign and beach over your shoulder. For a more tropical look, stand under the coconut palms on the Vo Nguyen Giap Street sidewalks.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pedestrian bridge in East Sea Park, right next to My Khe Beach, while you pose with the sea and sand behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch the flags, because rip currents happen here, and stay out of the water while you're looking at your screen. Stay in the public areas, keep an eye on your belongings, and check local rules before flying a drone.
card.challenge: Find a boat or a fisherman, line the horizon up with a gridline, and see if you can get the sun, the boat and the sea into one frame.
card.good_to_know: My Khe is a long public city beach, and it's free to visit. From the sand you can see Son Tra Peninsula with the Lady Buddha statue on the mountain. Công viên Biển Đông nearby has a carp-turned-dragon statue against the sea.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the beach stretch in front of Võ Nguyên Giáp street, near the Fusion Maia resort entrance. Face the open sea, with Son Tra Peninsula in the distance.

card.hook: Picture a 666 m steel dragon stretched across the Han River, glowing after dark and looking very pleased with itself. It's hard to take a bad photo of it, so you may as well take a good one.
card.stand_here: Head to the riverside promenade on Bạch Đằng, on the city-centre (west) bank. Walk to the promenade edge and face the bridge so you see the whole dragon side-on across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bridge and the skyline in one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched look. Zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, picks out the dragon's head and the lights along its back.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then drag the slider to make it slightly darker so the lights don't burn out against the night sky.
card.best_time: Go around dusk and into the evening, when the bridge is lit and its reflections show up on the water. The fire and water show is listed for Saturday and Sunday at 9 pm, and it may run on Fridays too, so check locally. Arrive early, because the riverbank fills up fast.
card.selfie_here: Stand mid-span on Love Bridge, next to the Dragon Bridge, with the dragon's lights glowing in the distance behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the colourful love locks fill the foreground. The dragon will look small from here, but the lights make a lovely backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Bạch Đằng promenade about 150 m from the dragon, and you stand a few steps ahead of them so the whole dragon fits behind you at a three-quarter angle.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep clear of the bridge deck and the dragon's mouth, because some visitors report spray and the deck is closed to traffic shortly before the show.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the bridge along the lower third and its reflection wobbling in the water in front. Then see if you can catch a flame in the next one.
card.good_to_know: The Dragon Bridge (Cầu Rồng) is described as the world's largest dragon-shaped steel bridge. It's 666 m long and 37.5 m wide, with six traffic lanes. The main span was finished in October 2012, and the bridge opened to traffic on 29 March 2013.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the riverside promenade on Bạch Đằng, on the city-centre (west) bank. Walk to the promenade edge and face the bridge so you see the whole dragon side-on across the water.

selfie_spots.why: This is the one selfie spot a page ties to a clear view of the dragon's lights, and the bridge's own colourful love locks make a strong foreground.

selfie_research.notes: Sources disagree on which bank is which: Vietnam Tourism calls the Tran Hung Dao side the east bank, while Localgrapher places the Bach Dang waterfront on the eastern side of the bridge. The ask-someone spot therefore needs a check on the map. The Furama 'underneath' spot and the Love Bridge spot come from one blog only, and the Love Bridge view shows the dragon only in the distance. Vietnam Tourism advises against standing on the bridge deck because of motorbikes and selfie sticks; this is a comment, not a rule. The Furama page recommends tripods or selfie sticks for night shots, but it gives no rule on them. No page states a rule on selfie sticks or tripods. The show is on weekends around 9pm, and sources say the riverbank fills quickly.

card.hook: Everyone lines up at Han Market's front door, but the better picture is round the side. The narrow lane has drink stalls, hair-salon shopfronts and a slightly scruffy charm.
card.stand_here: Stand on Nguyễn Thái Học, the narrow lane that runs alongside the market's side wall. Face along the lane so the wall, the stalls and the salon fronts all line up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the lane and wall as people see it. If the lane feels too tight, tap 0.5x to fit the wall and shopfronts in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a stall, a cup or a sign, so you can stay back from the vendors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the wall and doorways straight, then tap the stall and slide a little darker if bright sky or shopfronts wash out.
card.best_time: No best time is known for this spot, so go whenever suits you. The lane is ordinary street life, so there's no wrong moment.
card.selfie_here: Head to the main entrance at 119 Tran Phu Street and stand in front of it, with the neon signs and golden lettering behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the old-school sign fill the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On Bach Dang Street, on the river-side frontage of the market, ask a passer-by to photograph you in front of the market with the lantern-lit night market in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the market, but ask vendors before close-ups of them or their goods. Keep to the edge of the lane so you don't block people, and bring a hat for the sun.
card.challenge: Find a drink stall, a cup and a salon doorway, then get all three into one photo with a passer-by sitting on one third of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Han Market is a busy everyday market in central Da Nang, and the lane beside it has an old-fashioned feel that changes little. The Dragon Bridge is about 950 m away. The main Trần Phú-side entrance isn't always open, and a side door on Yên Bái street may be needed instead.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Nguyễn Thái Học, the narrow lane that runs alongside the market's side wall. Face along the lane so the wall, the stalls and the salon fronts all line up in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a 67 m Lady Buddha standing over the sea, with the bay and a forested hillside lined up behind her. Your phone has to work hard to miss this one.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, then climb to the upper terrace at the Lady Buddha's lotus base. Stand at the far right (east) side and face across the statue towards the open sea.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main shot of the statue with the sea behind. Go to 0.5x when you're close to the base and want the whole statue and the lotus terrace in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gate, Xa Loi Tower or the coastline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out the sea and the statue's details.
card.best_time: Go in the morning if you can. The light is soft and the sun hasn't hit the statue directly yet.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone slightly low and out in front. That way the big landmark sits over your shoulder instead of being cut off.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of worship, so photograph with respect. Photography inside the prayer halls is often restricted, so look for signs. Skip the flash, and don't stand in front of shrines or block pathways for a shot.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one vertical line, keep the horizon dead level, then take a second shot of her framed through the arch of the Cổng Tam Quan gate.
card.good_to_know: Linh Ung Pagoda (Chùa Linh Ứng Bãi Bụt) is a working Buddhist complex on the coast of Da Nang, looking over the East Sea and Da Nang Bay. Xa Loi Tower, a multi-storey relic tower with the ocean behind it, is often quieter than the statue. The statue's exact coordinates differ between map pages, so check the phone icon on the map before you start walking.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, then climb to the upper terrace at the Lady Buddha's lotus base. Stand at the far right (east) side and face across the statue towards the open sea.

card.hook: Most people come for the carved stone gods and dancers, but the building is a sight in its own right. It opened in 1919 and has been added to twice since, so the walls tell a story too.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map. It sits right at the Museum of Cham Sculpture, so you're in position the moment you arrive. Walk around the grounds, face the front of the building and step back until the whole thing fits.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the whole building and its grounds. Stay at 1x for most other shots, then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to get close to carved details without leaning over anything.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's upright edges so it doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Outside, morning or late afternoon gives softer light. Inside, the light is much the same all day, so pick a quieter time and you'll have the galleries (and your angles) to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Try the museum courtyard, under the frangipani tree in front of the terracotta-yellow arches. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the arches fill the space behind your shoulder. The street-side façade also works if you want the whole building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are fine in most areas. Selfie sticks need staff permission, and some guides say they're not allowed at all, so check at the door. Keep a respectful distance from the artefacts and don't block other visitors, and follow any signs in each room.
card.challenge: Find one carved face, fill your screen with it against a plain wall, then take a second shot with a hand or a pattern from the same piece. Which one tells the better story?
card.good_to_know: The museum is in Hải Châu District, close to the Han River, and is described as holding the world's largest collection of Cham sculpture. Two French architects designed the first building, encouraged by archaeologist Henri Parmentier to bring in traditional Cham elements. It was extended in the mid-1930s and again in 2002. Check the official site for tickets and opening hours before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map. It sits right at the Museum of Cham Sculpture, so you're in position the moment you arrive. Walk around the grounds, face the front of the building and step back until the whole thing fits.

card.hook: Most bridges just sit there. This one turns sideways in the middle of the river so boats can slip past, and it's the only swing bridge still working in Vietnam. Not a bad thing to have in your holiday photos.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Bạch Đằng riverside promenade on the west bank and face east across the Hàn River, straight at the bridge. For blue hour, guides like the stretch between the Hàn River Bridge and the Dragon Bridge, facing southeast.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the bridge, river and skyline all fit. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and cables.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, turn on night mode, rest your elbows on something solid, tap the bridge, and slide the brightness down a touch so the lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Blue hour is the sweet spot, with the sky still blue and the bridge lights on: about 6:00-6:30 PM in winter and 6:30-7:00 PM in summer. If you stay late, the bridge swings open for boats, but times vary, so check locally and arrive 20 to 30 minutes early.
card.selfie_here: Head for the riverside park along Bạch Đằng Street and turn your back to the water, so the lit-up bridge glows behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the bridge in, and keep your head to one side so the bridge shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a wide shot of you with the whole bridge, ask a passer-by to help from the west bank where Lê Duẩn Street begins, by the city square.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is an open public space and needs no ticket, but check locally for swing times and any temporary closures. Skip the bridge deck itself, because it's a poor place to photograph the bridge.
card.challenge: Catch the bridge lights wobbling in the water, with you grinning in one corner of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Hàn River Bridge opened on 29 March 2000. Its swing span is 122.7 metres long and turns on a round pier in the middle of the river. It's on Da Nang's city logo, so it makes a perfect 'I was in Da Nang' photo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Bạch Đằng riverside promenade on the west bank and face east across the Hàn River, straight at the bridge. For blue hour, guides like the stretch between the Hàn River Bridge and the Dragon Bridge, facing southeast.

card.hook: Monkey Mountain's best trick is at the top: the whole city of Da Nang spread out below you like a map, with dark green slopes filling the front of your shot. It's a short walk from the road, and the view is worth the puffing.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in the summit area of the peninsula's highest ridge at Ban Co Peak, close to the chessboard stone at the top. Face out over Da Nang Bay, My Khe Beach and the city.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bay and city. Switch to 0.5x to bring the forested slopes into the foreground, or try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out My Khe Beach.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky, then drag the slider down a little so the picture gets darker and the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go for sunrise, which guides pick as the best moment on the peak. On a clear day you might also spot Hai Van Pass, Lien Chieu Bay, Ba Na Hills and the Cham Islands.
card.selfie_here: Pose at the stone chessboard and the seated statue at the top of Ban Co Peak, using the front camera at 0.5x with the wide view behind you. If you visit Linh Ung Pagoda too, the terrace beside the foot of the 67 m Lady Buddha is the top photo spot there, with the statue above you and the bay below.
card.ask_someone: In the front courtyard of Linh Ung Pagoda, ask someone to stand well back across the courtyard while you stand in front of the Lady Buddha, so the full 67 m statue fits against the sea (keep it quick, it's a working temple).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to public areas: the radar station area is military and photography there may be restricted. If you see langurs, keep your distance and don't approach or feed them. At the pagoda, don't climb on statues or plinths, don't photograph people who are praying, and cover your shoulders and knees. Stay away from cliff edges.
card.challenge: Find the chessboard stone and fit it into a bottom corner of your shot, with the whole city stretching out behind it.
card.good_to_know: Ban Co means Chessboard, which is why there's a chessboard stone at the top. The mountain has been a nature reserve since 1992, covering about 26 square kilometres. It's home to the red-shanked douc langur, so you may see wildlife as well as views.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in the summit area of the peninsula's highest ridge at Ban Co Peak, close to the chessboard stone at the top. Face out over Da Nang Bay, My Khe Beach and the city.

card.hook: A bright pink church with a rooster perched on its bell tower: Da Nang Cathedral hardly needs help to look good on a phone. Even a quick snap comes out cheerful.
card.stand_here: Stand on Trần Phú, on the opposite side of the street, straight across from the front gate, and face west toward the cathedral. You'll get the whole pink facade, the spire and the rooster tower in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the road, which fits the facade, spire and tower together. If traffic or railings stop you stepping back, try zoom 0.5x, and use zoom 2x or more to pick out the rooster.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pink facade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays blue and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go before 9 a.m., when the light is soft and there are fewer people about.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the main front gate on Trần Phú, using the front camera, with the pink facade and spire rising behind you. Hold the phone a bit low, or try zoom 0.5x, to squeeze in more of the building.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement straight across Trần Phú from the front gate while you pose at the gate, because the pavement by the gate is crowded.
card.rules_and_safety: Take your photo from the pavement and never step into the traffic. The gates are locked during Mass, at lunch and sometimes on Sundays, and photos inside are not allowed during services. Renovation work may block some angles.
card.challenge: Can you get the rooster, the spire and a palm tree in one frame without a single scooter sneaking in?
card.good_to_know: Da Nang Cathedral is a pink church with a tall spire and a bell tower topped with a rooster. If the gates are open, there's a Lourdes-style grotto with religious statues in the courtyard. A back gate is sometimes open when the main one is shut.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Trần Phú, on the opposite side of the street, straight across from the front gate, and face west toward the cathedral. You'll get the whole pink facade, the spire and the rooster tower in one frame.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: the best photo of Love Lock Bridge starts at a giant fish that's turning into a dragon. Do the statue first, then the bridge.
card.stand_here: Stand at the base of Tượng Cá Chép Hóa Rồng, the carp-turned-dragon statue on Trần Hưng Đạo, where the map's stand-here point sits (check on the day). Crouch low beside the base and face up at the statue, with the sky behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole statue and a bit of its surroundings fit in. Switch to 1x for the lantern rows and railings, and if your phone has 2x or 5x, try it from the bridge to squash the padlocks and lanterns into a tight pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the statue, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the statue keeps its detail, and use the gridlines to keep it standing straight.
card.best_time: Go when the sky is blue, or at sunset, usually roughly 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. (check the time on the day). Weekend evenings get crowded around Dragon Bridge's 9 p.m. show, so come earlier for a clean statue shot.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the middle of the Love Lock Bridge and pose beside the heart-shaped lampposts, which is the favourite photo spot on the bridge. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the lampposts behind your shoulder, or stand on the walkway under the red heart lanterns with the Han River behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bridge entrance on the Trần Hưng Đạo side and aim at the centre while you stand on the bridge, so the whole row of heart lanterns stretches out behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Be careful crossing the roads around Trần Hưng Đạo Street, especially after the Dragon Bridge show when traffic gets busy. It looks like an open public riverside space, but check locally for any restrictions.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get the statue looking like it's about to launch itself into the sky.
card.good_to_know: Love Lock Bridge (Cầu Tình Yêu) has padlocked railings and rows of heart-shaped lanterns along the river. The statue beside it shows a carp turning into a dragon. Dragon Bridge is visible further along the river, and its fire-and-water show is reported for 9 p.m. at weekends.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the base of Tượng Cá Chép Hóa Rồng, the carp-turned-dragon statue on Trần Hưng Đạo, where the map's stand-here point sits (check on the day). Crouch low beside the base and face up at the statue, with the sky behind it.

card.hook: Picture a giant white sail leaning over the Hàn River, with its twin hanging upside down in the water below. That's Trần Thị Lý Bridge, and from the riverbank the whole thing fits in one frame.
card.stand_here: Head for Bạch Đằng, the riverside stretch along the Hàn River bank near the bridge. Face the bridge, which lies to the east of you, and walk back far enough to fit the tower and its reflection in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the bridge, its reflection and the skyline all in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the tower, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the cables fanning from the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness a little darker so the lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, when the bridge's LED lights come on and the reflections are at their strongest. After dark, use night mode and keep your elbows tucked against your body to hold still.
card.selfie_here: Try the skylight underpass at the west end of the bridge, where sunlight through the skylight makes bold light-and-shadow patterns for a close selfie with the bridge overhead. Or use the stone walkway at the foot of the bridge on the east bank at sunrise, when the sail-shaped tower catches the golden light. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the bridge in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the neighbouring Nguyễn Văn Trỗi Bridge, if it's open to walkers (check on site), so they can frame the full tower and cables with you in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: The skylight underpass is busy with vehicles, so stand close to the curb and don't block traffic. Take your photos from the bank, not the traffic deck, and check local signs.
card.challenge: Get the tower, its reflection and a perfectly level deck in one shot, with not a single walker in the frame. Be patient and wait for the gap.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened on 29 March 2013 and is 731 metres long and 145 metres tall. It replaced two older bridges and stands where Da Nang's first bridge was built in 1951. That bridge has had several names, including Trần Thị Lý from 1975.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Bạch Đằng, the riverside stretch along the Hàn River bank near the bridge. Face the bridge, which lies to the east of you, and walk back far enough to fit the tower and its reflection in.

card.hook: Picture a bridge so long that your phone has to squint: 1,850 metres of deck, two 80-metre towers, and a river that runs out into the sea right behind it. This is Vietnam's longest suspension bridge, and it loves being photographed.
card.stand_here: Head to the riverside promenade on Đường Như Nguyệt, on the west bank of the Han River, upstream of the bridge. Stand at the water's edge and face the bridge, so you see it from below and across the river.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole bridge over the water. Try 0.5x for more sky and river, but keep the bridge in the middle so the edges don't stretch it. Zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) picks out the towers and cables.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the waterline on the lower third so the reflection fills the bottom of the picture, and line the towers up with the vertical lines.
card.best_time: Go at night, when the bridge is lit up and its reflection shimmers on the water. Sunset also works, but guides disagree on the exact time, so arrive a little early.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the Han River embankment at the foot of Thuận Phước Bridge, where the bridge rises behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the bridge over your shoulder, and take a quick look around when you arrive to find the best spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Như Nguyệt promenade, where the full span of the bridge is visible, to take your photo with the bridge behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the port waterfront may be restricted, so check the official site before you go. If you wander onto the bridge itself, keep an eye on the traffic.
card.challenge: Get both towers standing straight and the reflection filling the bottom of the frame, with no sagging deck.
card.good_to_know: Thuận Phước Bridge has a main span of 405 metres and is 18 metres wide. Building began in 2003 and it was inaugurated on 19 July 2009. It crosses the mouth of the Han River, close to the Tiên Sa port area and the green slopes of Sơn Trà.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the riverside promenade on Đường Như Nguyệt, on the west bank of the Han River, upstream of the bridge. Stand at the water's edge and face the bridge, so you see it from below and across the river.
